lesson.grammar_point: modal verbs for obligation, permission and advice

listenings.text: Luiz, it's Sandra from compliance, about the Rezende file. You may approve up to the agreed limit, because they are an existing customer. You may not go above it. Anything above the limit has to go to the finance director, and she is away until Monday. If there is collateral in that file, legal must sign off before you release anything. And you should put the sixty-day request in writing today. You do not have to decide today. You do have to record it.

Luiz, Marco. Two rules before you answer Rezende. You must not release new product on any account that is more than ninety days overdue. That rule is not mine and I cannot change it. Second, verbal approval does not exist here. If somebody tells you on the telephone that it is fine, you should ask them to send it in writing, and you may say that I told you to. You are allowed to be the difficult one. That is the job.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: being officially allowed to do something
a limit on what somebody is allowed to do
legal responsibility for a loss, if something goes wrong
something you have to do, whether you want to or not
something valuable a customer offers in case they cannot pay
a rule written by a government or an official body
the agreed set of steps a company follows to get something done
to give somebody official approval to do something

paras: Anybody who has to refuse things for a living learns two lessons in the first year, and they sound like they contradict each other. The first is that a written limit is a gift. If there is no rule, every refusal is personal: the customer believes you decided, and he remembers it next season. If there is a rule, the sentence changes shape. I am not allowed to approve that at this level is not a softer no; it is a different kind of no, one that nobody has to take personally and nobody has to lose face over. That is what a procedure is actually for, and it is why calling it bureaucracy misses the point most of the time.

The second lesson is that the same no has to be said in two completely different ways, and the difference is not politeness. It is who has to do something with your answer. To a family farm you have known for twenty years, you say it plainly, on the telephone, and you say what you can do instead. A formal letter to that man reads as a threat, whatever it says. To a large distributor you do the reverse: it goes in writing, it names the clause, and it uses the flat institutional forms on purpose. We are not able to authorize an increase at this stage is not coldness. The person reading it has to forward it to somebody above them, and a warm, vague message is useless for that.

English does most of this work with a very small set of words. Must and have to carry obligation, and they are not identical: must tends to come from the speaker, have to from the situation or the rules. Should and ought to give advice rather than orders. Can, may and could open and close the door on permission, with may and could sitting higher up the formal scale. And one pair catches almost every learner: you do not have to and you must not are opposites, not variations. You do not have to send the report today means it is optional. You must not send the report today means it is forbidden. Getting that pair wrong with a customer who owes you money is not a grammar mistake. It is a commercial one.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: Written rules should be avoided because customers experience them as bureaucracy.
A written limit makes a refusal impersonal, and the same refusal has to change register depending on who has to act on it.
The formal register is always the safer choice with any customer.

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: I am not allowed to approve that at this level.
You do not have to decide today, but I must have an answer by Friday.
We are not able to authorize an increase at this stage.
I think you should talk to the dealer before the harvest.
